paras: The shooting of John Wells was the wounding of a Black porter by Charles Highland, a merchant policeman, in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of October 14, 1903. Highland took Wells for a burglar and fired without warning, striking him twice in the right leg. The Indianapolis Journal reported the case as the shooting of "an Innocent Man" by an officer "too ready with a pistol."

Wells was described as "a colored porter in the Wellington flats, on Michigan street." On the night of the shooting he was in the cellar of the Conservatory of Music on North Illinois street, doing some work for the institution.

Highland saw Wells enter the building and supposed him to be a thief. According to the Journal, he drew his revolver and fired "without asking any questions or giving any warning." Two bullets struck Wells in the right leg and lodged in the muscles. Highland afterward said he had been excited when he fired and admitted that he had not tried to learn who the "supposed intruder" was.

Wells was taken in the Dispensary ambulance to 521 Scioto street, where Dr. Jeffries attended him and the bullets were extracted. No report of an arrest, charge or inquiry concerning Highland appears in the coverage, and Wells's later condition is not reported.

The only account found is a short item on page 12 of the Indianapolis Journal of October 15, 1903. Its headline, "TOO READY WITH A PISTOL," and its deck, "Charles Highland, Merchant Police man, Shoots an Innocent Man," placed the fault on the officer. The text stressed Wells's legitimate errand and Highland's own admission, while identifying Wells by race as "a colored porter" and "the negro" and leaving Highland unmarked. No coverage of the shooting was found in the Black press or in other white papers.
